n: The fourth acrostic opens again with “How…!” Gold has lost its shine and sacred stones lie scattered in the streets—pictures of Jerusalem’s lost glory and perhaps of its precious people.

f.g: Literally “holy stones”; possibly temple stones, or a metaphor for the people themselves (see v. 2).

n: Zion’s children, once valued like pure gold, are now treated like cheap clay jars that are easily broken and thrown away.

f.w: earthen pitchers, the work of the hands of the potter

n: Even wild animals nurse their young, but famine has made Jerusalem’s mothers unable to care for their children, like the ostrich that was thought to abandon its eggs.

f.g: Probably jackals; the Hebrew tannim is close to the word for jackals.

f.w: like the ostriches in the wilderness

n: Nursing babies are so thirsty their tongues stick to their mouths; children beg for bread and no one has any to give.

f.g: Breaks bread to share it out.

n: People who once ate fine food now starve in the streets; those raised in royal purple now cling to garbage heaps. Wealth offered no protection.

f.g: Expensive dyed clothing, a sign of luxury.
Refuse or ash heaps where the destitute sat.

n: Jerusalem’s punishment seems worse than Sodom’s, which was destroyed in a moment; Jerusalem’s suffering dragged on. Her privileged knowledge made her sin greater.
Her consecrated ones (or princes) were once radiant—whiter than milk, ruddy and healthy, gleaming like precious stones.

f.g: Those set apart by a special vow, or more broadly her nobles. Nazarite vows are described in Numbers 6.
Probably lapis lazuli, a deep blue stone.

n: Now their faces are blackened and unrecognizable, their skin shriveled on their bones like dry wood. Famine has erased their glory.
Those killed in battle were better off than those who slowly starved to death—a grim measure of the siege’s horror.
Compassionate mothers boiled their own children for food—the darkest horror of the siege, exactly as Moses had warned would happen if Israel broke the covenant.

f.w: The hands of the pitiful women have sodden their own children

n: The Lord has fully carried out his anger. A fire in Zion has burned down to the foundations—both literally, when Babylon burned the city, and spiritually.

f.w: hath kindled a fire in Zion

n: No one in the world would have believed Jerusalem could fall. Many in Judah had trusted the temple would make the city untouchable.
The cause of the disaster: the sins of prophets and priests who shed innocent blood—the very leaders who should have guided the people to God.

f.w: For the sins of her prophets
shed the blood of the just

n: These guilty leaders now stagger through the streets like blind men, stained with blood so that no one will touch their clothing.
People shout at them as they would at lepers: “Unclean! Stay away!” Even among foreign nations they are told they cannot stay.
The Lord himself has scattered them. Since they showed no respect for priests and elders, honor is now withheld from them.
“We” now speak: we kept watching for an ally nation—Egypt—to rescue us, but it never could.

f.w: a nation that could not save us

n: Enemies tracked every step until no one could walk safely; the end had arrived.
The pursuers were faster than eagles, chasing them over the mountains and ambushing them in the wilderness.
King Zedekiah, “the Lord’s anointed,” on whom the people pinned their hopes, was captured as he fled. The phrase “breath of our nostrils” shows how central the king was to national life.
Bitterly, the poet tells Edom to celebrate for now—Edom cheered Jerusalem’s fall—but the cup of God’s judgment will pass to her too.

f.g: Descendants of Esau, southeast of Judah; they helped and gloated over Jerusalem’s fall.

n: A word of hope: Zion’s punishment is complete, and her exile will not continue forever. Edom’s sins, however, will now be exposed and punished.

f.w: The punishment of thine iniquity is accomplished
